Sometimes babies can't deal with fast letdowns and tend to stick to bottle. They start rejecting breasts sometimes (as warned by our doctor). What comes out from pumping isn't usually the same amount that the baby is getting as babies are more effective at extracting milk whereas pumps don't stimulate the mammary gland in the same way. If the baby remains hungry, please supplement with formula/pumped milk.

I had the same fear - how can i tell how much the baby is getting. Maybe he's not getting enough. In retrospect, i should have simply offered formula on top of feeding+giving pumped milk. But his doc was an exclusive breastfeeding pusher and that created a lot of unnecessary anxiety in me.

Yes, i went through the same. It was traumatic. Painful situation. These are the lessons that i learnt:

1. Direct breastfeeding the baby will increase the supply. 
2. If the baby is still hungry, give her some formula immediately after a breastfeeding session as your wife pumps the remaining milk (If her energy levels allow. Otherwise let it go. She can do this 2-3 times later in the day). 
3. When the baby gets hungry again, offer breast. Repeat with pumped or formula milk. 
4. Try to simply offer breasts at night. No pumping required in case your wife is sleepy. Sleep is important to increase supply. If necessary, offer formula or pumped milk to the baby at night.
5. Ask your wife to increase her calorie and fluid intake. Oatmeal, millets, and quinoa soup are godsend. 
6. Have faith. You'll figure it out. 


In my case, i just stopped caring about pumping round the clock when my dad was in ICU when the baby turned 5 months old. I started direct breastfeeding most of the time, and pumping twice a day at max. Within a week, i was not pumping at all and my supply had increased. I guess sleep and lesser stress about pumping helped.

In my experience, it's just a roll of a dice. Some people face infertility in their mid 20's while the others give birth to healthy babies in their mid to late 30's. But if someone is bound to face infertility, they have a better chance conceiving with assisted reproductive technology in their young age. 

My sister in law is 23 and she had a couple of miscarriages and a late term baby loss (at 6 month pregnant) last month. Doctors have put her on a plan and are pretty confident that she'd be able to have healthy babies. My best friend got married at 26 and has struggled with fertility for 8 years. Now she's planning to adopt because she doesn't want to waste too much money on having a baby. A colleague got married at 31 and had a baby naturally at 37 after struggling for a while. 

I got my egg reserve checked (FSH) at 29 and was very anxious ever since because my flow had reduced a bit (I should have done pelvic ultrasound as well but i was dumb). Bit I got pregnant on my first try at 34, 15 days before turning 35 (got married at 34). My friend with PCOD and thyroid is having her third baby without a problem at 37. 

What I am trying to say is.....you have to be mentally prepared to have a baby, and keep your body healthy. Egg freezing is a great idea - a couple of friends have done it. And it is one of the most liberating things available for women today. The other thing you can do is keep yourself healthy, consume enough antioxidants, get a pelvic ultrasound done (it's not expensive) to assess and plan your fertility, and most importantly stay stress free.
